blocks.content: 1. Introduction

Every computer has a clock, and every clock lies a little. Not because the hardware is broken, but because physics and engineering make it impossible to keep two independent clocks perfectly in step. In a single machine this barely matters. In a distributed system spread across racks, data centers, and continents, it becomes one of the most subtle and dangerous sources of bugs an engineer will ever meet.

Clock skew is the difference between what one machine believes the current time is and what another machine believes it is, at the same physical instant. It sounds like a small detail. In practice it can silently corrupt the ordering of events, break assumptions in databases, and produce bugs that only show up under load, across regions, or after a network hiccup.
Clock skew is the gap between two clocks that both think they are correct.

This lesson walks through why clocks drift, why the usual fix of Network Time Protocol synchronization is not enough on its own, what goes wrong when you order events by wall clock timestamp, and two different ways engineers have solved the problem in real systems: Google Spanner TrueTime, which embraces uncertainty and waits it out, and Lamport timestamps, which sidestep physical time entirely and track causality instead.

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.content: Clock skew questions show up constantly in distributed systems interviews because they test whether a candidate actually understands the difference between what a system observes and what actually happened. It is a favorite follow up question after any design involving multiple nodes writing data.
2. Why Clocks Drift

Every server has a local oscillator, usually a quartz crystal, that ticks at a nominal frequency. Software counts these ticks to advance the system clock. The problem is that no two crystals tick at exactly the same rate, even if they came off the same factory line.
2.1 Crystal oscillator error

A typical quartz crystal used in servers has a frequency tolerance of around ten to twenty parts per million. That sounds tiny, but it adds up fast. Ten parts per million means the clock can drift by about one second every day. Multiply that across thousands of machines in a fleet, and every single one is drifting at a slightly different rate, in a slightly different direction.

["Temperature changes the resonant frequency of the crystal, so a hot server room can drift differently than a cool one.","Manufacturing variance means no two crystals, even the same model, tick at exactly the same rate.","Aging causes the crystal frequency to shift slowly over months and years.","Voltage fluctuations and mechanical vibration introduce small additional errors."]
items: Temperature changes the resonant frequency of the crystal, so a hot server room can drift differently than a cool one.
Manufacturing variance means no two crystals, even the same model, tick at exactly the same rate.
Aging causes the crystal frequency to shift slowly over months and years.
Voltage fluctuations and mechanical vibration introduce small additional errors.

blocks.content: 2.2 Why this becomes a distributed systems problem
blocks.text: 2.2 Why this becomes a distributed systems problem

blocks.content: On a single machine, drift is invisible because every process reads the same local clock, so relative ordering of events on that machine is always correct. The trouble starts the moment two different machines each stamp events with their own local clock and those timestamps get compared against each other.

If server A drifts one second fast and server B drifts one second slow over a day, the two clocks can be two seconds apart by the end of it, without any hardware failure and without anyone making a mistake. That two second gap is clock skew, and it is a completely normal, expected property of physical clocks, not an edge case.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785286924877-749364218.png
blocks.alt: Two server clocks starting in sync and drifting apart over time by tens of milliseconds

blocks.title: A useful mental model
blocks.content: Think of every machine clock as a slightly inaccurate wristwatch. It is fine for telling you roughly what time it is. It is not fine for deciding, down to the millisecond, who pressed a buzzer first in a room full of people each wearing a different watch.
2.3 Monotonic clocks measure durations, not timestamps
blocks.text: 2.3 Monotonic clocks measure durations, not timestamps

blocks.content: Most operating systems actually expose two different clocks. The wall clock, sometimes called real time, tells you what the current date and time is, and it can jump backward if an administrator corrects it or an NTP sync steps it. The monotonic clock only ever moves forward, has no relationship to the calendar, and is meant purely for measuring how much time has elapsed between two points on the same machine.

blocks.title: A rule worth memorizing
blocks.content: Use the monotonic clock whenever you are measuring a duration, for example a request timeout or a retry backoff, on a single machine. Use the wall clock only for timestamps that need to be meaningful to a human or compared across machines, and remember that comparison across machines is exactly where clock skew lives.
3. NTP and Its Limits

The Network Time Protocol, or NTP, is the standard way machines correct their local clock against a more authoritative time source. A client periodically asks a time server what time it is, estimates the network round trip delay, and nudges its own clock toward the answer.
3.1 How an NTP sync works

["The client records its own local time and sends a request to the NTP server.","The NTP server timestamps the request on arrival and again when it sends the reply.","The client records the time the reply arrives and now has four timestamps.","From those four timestamps it estimates the round trip delay and the offset between the two clocks.","The client adjusts its local clock, either by stepping it directly or by slowly slewing the rate so time never appears to jump backward."]
items: The client records its own local time and sends a request to the NTP server.
The NTP server timestamps the request on arrival and again when it sends the reply.
The client records the time the reply arrives and now has four timestamps.
From those four timestamps it estimates the round trip delay and the offset between the two clocks.
The client adjusts its local clock, either by stepping it directly or by slowly slewing the rate so time never appears to jump backward.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785286928189-962916451.png
blocks.alt: An NTP client drifting, syncing with a reference server, then drifting again before the next sync

blocks.content: 3.2 Typical accuracy

On a well configured local network, NTP can typically get clocks within one to ten milliseconds of each other. Across the public internet, with variable network paths and congestion, the error commonly grows to tens of milliseconds, and occasionally much worse if a network path is asymmetric or congested in one direction only.

3.3 Why NTP alone is not enough for strict ordering
blocks.text: 3.3 Why NTP alone is not enough for strict ordering

blocks.content: NTP reduces skew, it does not eliminate it, and critically it gives you no guaranteed bound on how wrong the clock might be at any given instant. A system that assumes NTP synced clocks are exact enough to order events millisecond by millisecond is making an assumption that NTP itself does not promise.

["Round trip delay is estimated, not measured exactly, and the estimate assumes a symmetric network path.","A congested or asymmetric network path silently introduces extra error that NTP cannot detect.","Virtual machines suffer from additional scheduling jitter that confuses the local clock further.","A single bad sync, a firewall blocking NTP traffic, or a misconfigured time zone can leave a machine far out of sync without any obvious alarm."]
items: Round trip delay is estimated, not measured exactly, and the estimate assumes a symmetric network path.
A congested or asymmetric network path silently introduces extra error that NTP cannot detect.
Virtual machines suffer from additional scheduling jitter that confuses the local clock further.
A single bad sync, a firewall blocking NTP traffic, or a misconfigured time zone can leave a machine far out of sync without any obvious alarm.

blocks.title: A concrete number to remember
blocks.content: A reasonable working assumption for machines in the same cloud region with healthy NTP is a few milliseconds of skew. Across regions, tens of milliseconds is common. Neither number is zero, and neither number is guaranteed.
3.4 Leap seconds add another wrinkle

Every year or two, the International Earth Rotation Service adds a leap second to keep the calendar aligned with the slowly changing rotation of the earth. That extra second does not fit neatly into a clock that counts sixty seconds per minute, and handling it badly has caused real outages.

["Some systems step the clock backward by one second at the leap second boundary, which can make an event appear to happen before an earlier event on the same machine.","Google popularized leap smearing, where the extra second is spread out in tiny slivers over an entire day so the clock never jumps or repeats a value.","A well known outage in 2012 took down several major websites when servers running an older Linux kernel entered a busy loop right at the leap second boundary."]
items: Some systems step the clock backward by one second at the leap second boundary, which can make an event appear to happen before an earlier event on the same machine.
Google popularized leap smearing, where the extra second is spread out in tiny slivers over an entire day so the clock never jumps or repeats a value.
A well known outage in 2012 took down several major websites when servers running an older Linux kernel entered a busy loop right at the leap second boundary.

blocks.title: Why this belongs in a clock skew discussion
blocks.content: Leap seconds are a reminder that clock trouble is not only about drift between machines. Even a single machine can have a broken notion of time for a moment, and any system that assumes wall clock time always moves forward in neat one second increments can be surprised.
4. Consequences for Ordering

The real danger of clock skew shows up the moment a system uses wall clock timestamps to decide the order in which events happened across different machines. If two machines disagree about what time it is, they can disagree about which event came first, even when one event clearly caused or preceded the other in reality.
4.1 The classic failure pattern

Imagine a write happens on server A, and shortly afterward a related write happens on server B, perhaps triggered by the first write through a message queue. If server A clock is running two seconds behind server B clock, the write on A can be stamped with a timestamp that is later than the write on B, even though A genuinely happened first in real time. Any system that sorts by timestamp will now report the events in the wrong order.

blocks.title: A payment system gone wrong
blocks.text: A user updates their shipping address on server A. A downstream service on server B reads the old address a moment later and logs a shipment confirmation. Server B clock is a little ahead. When support pulls the timeline sorted by timestamp, the address update appears to happen after the shipment confirmation, even though it happened first. The support engineer wrongly concludes the address change caused nothing and closes the ticket without noticing the real bug.

blocks.content: 4.2 Where this bites in real systems
blocks.text: 4.2 Where this bites in real systems

blocks.content: ["Last write wins conflict resolution in a distributed database can pick the wrong value if timestamps are skewed.","Log aggregation across services can present an event timeline that never actually happened in that order.","Distributed transactions that rely on timestamp ordering can violate serializability guarantees.","Cache invalidation logic keyed on timestamp can serve stale data if a slightly ahead clock wrote a newer looking but actually older value.","Audit trails and compliance logs can be legally meaningless if the recorded order does not match reality."]
items: Last write wins conflict resolution in a distributed database can pick the wrong value if timestamps are skewed.
Log aggregation across services can present an event timeline that never actually happened in that order.
Distributed transactions that rely on timestamp ordering can violate serializability guarantees.
Cache invalidation logic keyed on timestamp can serve stale data if a slightly ahead clock wrote a newer looking but actually older value.
Audit trails and compliance logs can be legally meaningless if the recorded order does not match reality.

blocks.alt: A naive system merges two server logs by timestamp and produces the wrong causal order because of clock skew

blocks.title: The core insight
blocks.content: A wall clock timestamp tells you when a machine believed something happened. It does not, on its own, tell you the true global order of events across machines. Those two things are easy to confuse and the confusion is where the bugs live.
5. TrueTime as a Real World Approach
blocks.text: 5. TrueTime as a Real World Approach

blocks.content: Google faced this exact problem while building Spanner, a globally distributed database that needed strict external consistency: if transaction one commits before transaction two starts, in real time, then transaction one must appear before transaction two to every reader, everywhere in the world. Ordinary timestamps with unknown error could not deliver that guarantee.
5.1 The key idea: stop pretending the clock is exact
blocks.text: 5.1 The key idea: stop pretending the clock is exact

blocks.content: Instead of trying to make clocks perfectly accurate, which is physically impossible, TrueTime does something clever. It makes the uncertainty explicit and bounded, then designs the system around that bound rather than ignoring it.

TrueTime exposes a single API call, commonly described as now, which does not return a single timestamp. It returns an interval, an earliest possible time and a latest possible time, guaranteed to contain the true current time somewhere inside it.
TrueTime never claims to know the exact time. It claims to know a window that definitely contains it.
5.2 How the interval stays small

["Each data center runs a set of time master servers equipped with GPS receivers and atomic clocks.","GPS gives accurate time but can fail during antenna issues or signal interference, atomic clocks drift slowly but predictably, so combining both sources covers each one weakness.","Local machines poll the time masters every thirty seconds or so and track their own local drift rate between polls.","The width of the uncertainty interval, commonly written as epsilon, typically stays around one to seven milliseconds in Google production reports."]
items: Each data center runs a set of time master servers equipped with GPS receivers and atomic clocks.
GPS gives accurate time but can fail during antenna issues or signal interference, atomic clocks drift slowly but predictably, so combining both sources covers each one weakness.
Local machines poll the time masters every thirty seconds or so and track their own local drift rate between polls.
The width of the uncertainty interval, commonly written as epsilon, typically stays around one to seven milliseconds in Google production reports.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396524933-617463577.png
blocks.alt: TrueTime returns an earliest and latest bound forming an uncertainty interval, and commit wait pauses until that interval has definitely passed

blocks.content: 5.3 Commit wait: turning uncertainty into a guarantee
blocks.text: 5.3 Commit wait: turning uncertainty into a guarantee

blocks.content: Knowing the uncertainty interval is not enough by itself. Spanner adds one more rule called commit wait. Before a transaction is allowed to become visible to other readers, Spanner waits until the earliest possible time of the commit timestamp interval has definitely passed according to TrueTime.

Because the wait is only as long as the uncertainty interval, and that interval is only a few milliseconds wide, the cost is small, typically single digit milliseconds of extra latency on a commit. In exchange, Spanner gets a hard guarantee that if transaction one finishes before transaction two starts in real wall clock time, their assigned timestamps will reflect that order correctly, everywhere.

blocks.title: Why this is a big deal
blocks.content: Commit wait is the piece most people miss. TrueTime alone only bounds the error. It is the deliberate act of waiting out that bound before committing that turns a bounded guess into a provable guarantee.
5.4 The cost of this approach

["Requires specialized hardware, GPS receivers and atomic clocks, in every data center.","Adds a small but real latency cost to every commit, proportional to the uncertainty interval.","Only Google, and a small number of companies with similar infrastructure investment, can realistically deploy this at the same scale."]
items: Requires specialized hardware, GPS receivers and atomic clocks, in every data center.
Adds a small but real latency cost to every commit, proportional to the uncertainty interval.
Only Google, and a small number of companies with similar infrastructure investment, can realistically deploy this at the same scale.

blocks.content: 6. Logical Clocks as an Alternative

Not every system can afford atomic clocks and GPS receivers in every rack. Long before TrueTime existed, Leslie Lamport proposed a completely different way of thinking about time in distributed systems: forget wall clock time altogether, and instead track causality directly.
6.1 The core idea

A Lamport clock is just a counter that every node keeps locally. It has nothing to do with the actual time of day. It only guarantees one property: if event one causally happened before event two, meaning event two could only have occurred because it learned about event one, then the Lamport timestamp of event one is smaller than the Lamport timestamp of event two.
A Lamport clock does not tell you what time it is. It tells you what happened before what.
6.2 The two simple rules

["Before executing any local event, a node increments its own counter by one.","When sending a message, a node attaches its current counter value to the message.","When receiving a message, a node sets its counter to the maximum of its own current value and the received value, then increments by one."]
items: Before executing any local event, a node increments its own counter by one.
When sending a message, a node attaches its current counter value to the message.
When receiving a message, a node sets its counter to the maximum of its own current value and the received value, then increments by one.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785286935511-283795782.png
blocks.alt: Two nodes exchange a message, and the receiving node advances its Lamport counter past the value it received

blocks.content: 6.3 A quick worked increment

Suppose node one is at counter value one and sends a message. Node two, independently, is also at counter value one. When node two receives the message carrying value one, it takes the maximum of its own one and the received one, which is one, then increments to two. Node two counter is now two, guaranteed to be greater than the counter value attached to the message it depended on.
6.4 What Lamport clocks give you, and what they do not
blocks.text: 6.4 What Lamport clocks give you, and what they do not

blocks.content: Lamport timestamps guarantee that causally related events are ordered correctly. They do not, however, tell you anything about events that are not causally related to each other, sometimes called concurrent events. Two nodes that never communicated might end up with the same Lamport timestamp, or with timestamps in an order that has no relationship to real wall clock time at all.

blocks.title: Vector clocks as an extension
blocks.content: When a system needs to detect concurrent, unrelated events rather than just order causally related ones, engineers often reach for vector clocks, which keep a counter per node instead of a single shared counter. That is a deeper topic in its own right, worth studying separately.
6.5 Hybrid Logical Clocks bridge the two worlds
blocks.text: 6.5 Hybrid Logical Clocks bridge the two worlds

blocks.content: Pure Lamport counters have one practical downside: a timestamp like seven tells you nothing about when, in human terms, an event happened. Operators still want to look at a log and see something resembling a real date and time.

A Hybrid Logical Clock, used in systems such as CockroachDB and MongoDB, solves this by pairing a physical wall clock reading with a logical counter that only advances when needed to preserve causal order. The physical part keeps timestamps close to real time and human readable, while the logical part guarantees that causally related events still sort correctly even if the physical clocks involved are skewed.

blocks.title: Where this fits
blocks.content: Think of a Hybrid Logical Clock as choosing a pragmatic middle ground. It does not need the atomic clocks and GPS receivers that TrueTime relies on, but it still produces timestamps that look like ordinary dates, unlike a bare Lamport counter.
7. Worked Example

Consider two servers, A and B, both logging user activity events into a shared log that gets merged and displayed to a support engineer. Server A clock is running two hundred milliseconds behind true time. Server B clock is running exactly on true time.
7.1 The sequence of real events

["At true time 10:00:00.000, a user clicks submit on server A. Server A, running two hundred milliseconds behind, logs this as 10:00:00.000 minus 0.200, meaning it stamps the event at 09:59:59.800.","At true time 10:00:00.100, a notification service on server B, triggered by that click through a queue, logs a follow up event. Server B clock is accurate, so it stamps this at 10:00:00.100."]
items: At true time 10:00:00.000, a user clicks submit on server A. Server A, running two hundred milliseconds behind, logs this as 10:00:00.000 minus 0.200, meaning it stamps the event at 09:59:59.800.
At true time 10:00:00.100, a notification service on server B, triggered by that click through a queue, logs a follow up event. Server B clock is accurate, so it stamps this at 10:00:00.100.

blocks.content: 7.2 What the naive merged log shows
blocks.text: 7.2 What the naive merged log shows

blocks.content: Sorting purely by wall clock timestamp, server A event at 09:59:59.800 appears before server B event at 10:00:00.100. This actually happens to be correct in this specific case, purely by luck. Now flip the skew direction and the story changes completely.

blocks.title: Flipping the skew direction
blocks.text: Suppose instead server A clock is two hundred milliseconds ahead rather than behind. The same click at true time 10:00:00.000 gets logged as 10:00:00.200. The notification on server B still logs at 10:00:00.100, accurately. Now the merged log shows the notification, the effect, appearing to happen fifty milliseconds before the click, the cause. A support engineer reading this log would conclude the notification fired for no reason, when in fact clock skew simply lied about the order.

blocks.content: 7.3 The same scenario with Lamport timestamps
blocks.text: 7.3 The same scenario with Lamport timestamps

blocks.content: Now redo this with Lamport clocks instead of wall clock time. Server A is at local counter five when the user clicks submit, so it logs the event with Lamport value six. It sends a message to the queue carrying that value. Server B receives the message, takes the maximum of its own counter and six, then increments, guaranteeing its logged event carries a Lamport value strictly greater than six, for example seven.

No matter how badly the physical clocks on A and B drift relative to each other, the Lamport values six and seven preserve the true causal order. The notification can never appear to precede the click that caused it, because the counter mechanics forbid it.

{"headers":["Approach","Server A event","Server B event","Correct causal order preserved"],"rows":[["Wall clock, A slow","09:59:59.800","10:00:00.100","Yes, by chance"],["Wall clock, A fast","10:00:00.200","10:00:00.100","No, order reversed"],["Lamport clock","value six","value seven","Yes, always"]]}

blocks.title: The lesson from this example
blocks.content: Wall clock ordering is correct only when skew happens to fall in a forgiving direction. Lamport ordering is correct by construction, every time, because it tracks the actual message that carried causality rather than trusting two independent clocks to agree.
8. Comparing the Approaches
Each approach to time in distributed systems makes a different trade off between accuracy, cost, and what guarantee it actually provides.

blocks.content: 9. Interview Angle

Clock skew is a favorite follow up question because it separates candidates who have only memorized system design patterns from candidates who understand the underlying physical reality those patterns are built on.
9.1 Questions you should expect

["Why can two synchronized servers still disagree on the current time.","What happens if you use timestamps alone to resolve write conflicts in a distributed database.","How does Spanner guarantee external consistency despite clock uncertainty.","What is the difference between a Lamport timestamp and a real wall clock timestamp.","When would you choose logical clocks over synchronized physical clocks, and why."]
items: Why can two synchronized servers still disagree on the current time.
What happens if you use timestamps alone to resolve write conflicts in a distributed database.
How does Spanner guarantee external consistency despite clock uncertainty.
What is the difference between a Lamport timestamp and a real wall clock timestamp.
When would you choose logical clocks over synchronized physical clocks, and why.

blocks.content: 9.2 A strong answer structure

Start by naming the root cause: independent oscillators drift at different rates, so no fleet of machines can share a perfectly identical clock. Then explain that NTP reduces but does not eliminate this error, and give a concrete number like a few milliseconds within a data center and tens of milliseconds across regions. Then connect it to the actual failure mode, timestamp based ordering can be wrong, with a specific example like last write wins conflict resolution picking the wrong value.

Finally, mention that there are two credible fixes with different trade offs: embrace and bound the uncertainty like TrueTime does, which needs special hardware and adds a small wait, or sidestep physical time entirely with logical clocks, which are cheap but only order causally related events, not truly concurrent ones.

blocks.title: A trap to avoid
blocks.content: Do not claim NTP solves clock skew. Interviewers listen closely for this. The correct framing is that NTP reduces the size of the problem, it does not remove the need to design around remaining uncertainty.
9.3 A common mistake to avoid

Many candidates jump straight to suggesting TrueTime as the universal fix. A stronger answer recognizes that TrueTime requires infrastructure investment that only a handful of companies can justify, and that logical clocks solve a large fraction of real ordering problems at essentially zero cost. Naming both options and picking the right one for the constraints in front of you demonstrates judgment, not just recall.
10. Summary

["Every machine clock drifts because oscillators are physically imperfect, and the drift is a normal property of hardware, not a bug.","NTP synchronization reduces skew to roughly single digit to double digit milliseconds but provides no hard guaranteed bound.","Ordering events by raw wall clock timestamp across machines can produce a causally wrong order, exactly backward from what actually happened.","Google Spanner TrueTime exposes an explicit uncertainty interval and uses commit wait to turn that bounded uncertainty into a provable global ordering guarantee.","Lamport logical clocks abandon physical time entirely and instead track causality directly through a simple counter passed along with every message.","Choosing between these approaches is a real engineering trade off between hardware cost, latency, and the strength of ordering guarantee actually needed."]
items: Every machine clock drifts because oscillators are physically imperfect, and the drift is a normal property of hardware, not a bug.
NTP synchronization reduces skew to roughly single digit to double digit milliseconds but provides no hard guaranteed bound.
Ordering events by raw wall clock timestamp across machines can produce a causally wrong order, exactly backward from what actually happened.
Google Spanner TrueTime exposes an explicit uncertainty interval and uses commit wait to turn that bounded uncertainty into a provable global ordering guarantee.
Lamport logical clocks abandon physical time entirely and instead track causality directly through a simple counter passed along with every message.
Choosing between these approaches is a real engineering trade off between hardware cost, latency, and the strength of ordering guarantee actually needed.

blocks.content: Clock skew is small in magnitude, usually just milliseconds, but large in consequence, because so many distributed systems quietly assume timestamps are trustworthy for ordering. Understanding why that assumption breaks, and the two very different ways real systems have fixed it, is a core piece of distributed systems literacy.
In a distributed system, agreeing on what time it is turns out to be almost as hard as agreeing on what happened.
